## THE CURRENT MAP
20:10/q01 How does the time clause 'when he saw' connect grammatically to the account? [إِذْ رَءَا · grammar] (turns on: Whether the preceding account has enough event sense to govern idh, or an unspoken command or event must be supplied.)
  20:10/q01/p1 It modifies the preceding account or report of Moses. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies the implicit action in ḥadīth; al-Ṭabrisī calls it an accusative circumstance; al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān treat the account as an event; al-Sharīf says story and report imply occurrence; al-Ālūsī prefers attachment to the preceding revealed account, since a bare substantive cannot govern the clause.
  20:10/q01/p2 It is the object of an implicit command to remember the time. — reasons: Abū al-Baqāʾ and al-Zamakhsharī are cited for the implied udhkur; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow it.
  20:10/q01/p3 It depends on an omitted following event or verb. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī is cited by al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī; al-Nasafī permits an omitted event.
20:10/q02 What journey and circumstances led Moses to see the fire? [إِذْ رَءَا نَارًۭا · reports] (turns on: The reports differ in how Moses lost the road and in the journey's particular circumstances.)
  20:10/q02/p1 Returning from Midian toward Egypt with his family, Moses lost the way on a cold dark night and could not kindle fire. — reasons: Muqātil and others specify winter, sometimes Friday, snow, pregnancy or a son's birth, dispersed livestock, no water, and fire to the left or on a mountain near Ṭuwā. Wahb says Shuʿayb allowed a visit to Moses' mother; some mention Aaron, the completed term, a flock and more than ten years away. Ibn Kathīr cites 28:29; al-Kuranyolu gives eight or ten years. The reports vary in these details.
  20:10/q02/p2 His protectiveness toward his wife led him to separate from companions and lose the route. — reasons: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says he avoided a group lest they see her; al-Baghawī says he joined caravans at night and separated by day; al-Qurṭubī says God decreed the separation. Some add detouring from Syrian rulers.
  20:10/q02/p3 The fire episode belongs to Moses' wanderings after fleeing Egypt. — reasons: Asad cites the sequence beginning at 28:14 and infers from 27:7 and 28:29 that Moses was lost in the desert.
20:10/q03 What did Moses actually see when the verse calls it fire? [نَارًۭا · referent] (turns on: Whether 'fire' names a physical fire, divine light perceived as fire, a small visible flame, or an allegorical image; al-Rāzī and Bursevī appeal to prophetic truthfulness.)
  20:10/q03/p1 He saw divine light that appeared to him to be fire. — reasons: Al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās and most exegetes distinguish Moses' perception from God's light; some call it the Lord's light. Al-Kuranyolu says the light drew him into God's presence. Al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān object that making it merely imagined fire threatens the truth of a prophet's report.
  20:10/q03/p2 It was real fire. — reasons: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr calls it one of God's veils and cites Abū Mūsā's report that the unveiled fire would burn creation within God's sight. Al-Rāzī and Bursevī prefer actual fire because prophets cannot lie; al-Rāzī says the verse does not establish that it was in a tree. Classifications distinguish Moses' fire as consuming neither food nor drink, or as luminous without burning, against worldly and infernal fires; 36:80 is cited.
  20:10/q03/p3 He saw a brief shimmering flame, perhaps visible only to him. — reasons: Iṣlāḥī reasons that a large blaze would have prompted a different description; Ṭabāṭabāʾ takes the emphatic report to imply that only Moses perceived it.
  20:10/q03/p4 The fire is an allegory of the burning bush. — reasons: Asad refers to the biblical burning bush and his note on 27:7–8.
20:10/q04 What was reported about the tree and fire as Moses approached? [نَارًۭا · reports] (turns on: Reports give different tree species and details of its behavior; al-Rāzī questions whether the Qurʾānic wording establishes any tree.)
  20:10/q04/p1 The fire appeared in a green tree and did not consume it. — reasons: Al-Baghawī describes brilliant white fire surrounding the tree from bottom to top without altering its green color; Ibn ʿAbbās marveled at its unchanged beauty. Al-Mahdawī says it receded as Moses approached, then drew near after fear. Al-Qushayrī says the tree burned end to end but yielded no flame and illuminated hearts, while al-Rāzī notes the Qurʾān does not establish the tree detail.
  20:10/q04/p2 The tree was a jujube or ʿanāb. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported for the jujube identification; Abū Ḥayyān's collected variants include ʿanāb.
  20:10/q04/p3 The tree was al-ʿawsaj, a thorn tree. — reasons: Qatāda, Muqātil and al-Kalbī are named by al-Baghawī; al-Mahdawī says a thorn tree.
  20:10/q04/p4 The tree was a green samura. — reasons: Al-Baghawī attributes this to Ibn Masʿūd; Abū Ḥayyān lists it among variants.
  20:10/q04/p5 The tree was al-ʿaliq or ʿalīqah. — reasons: Al-Baghawī reports Wahb's identification; Abū Ḥayyān lists the variant.
  20:10/q04/p6 Moses thought the distant light was a shepherd's fire. — reasons: Al-Suddī and Bursevī connect the expectation of a firebrand to shepherds.
20:10/q05 Who was Moses' 'family' whom he addressed? [لِأَهْلِهِ · referent] (turns on: Whether ahl includes children and a servant, or denotes the wife alone with plural wording.)
  20:10/q05/p1 His wife, children, and possibly a servant. — reasons: Al-Rāzī gives wife, child and servant; Abū Ḥayyān specifies wife, two sons and servant. Al-Ālūsī allows wife, child and servant. Ṭabāṭabāʾ infers others were present from the instruction to stay.
  20:10/q05/p2 His wife alone, Shuʿayb's daughter. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī explains the plural by ahl's collective outward form; al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī add respectful plural address. Al-Suhaylī names her Ṣafūriyya.
20:10/q06 What does 'stay' mean here? [ٱمْكُثُوٓا۟ · meaning]
  20:10/q06/p1 Remain here temporarily. — reasons: Al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī distinguish makth from iqāma, which implies continuing residence; other sources gloss it as stay or remain in place.
20:10/q07 Why did Moses tell his family to stay? [فَقَالَ لِأَهْلِهِ ٱمْكُثُوٓا۟ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the departure is explained by deliberate care for the family or an overwhelming response to the sight.)
  20:10/q07/p1 He wanted them to remain while he went to seek fire or directions. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī says he prevented them following him toward the fire, as people commonly do; Ṭabāṭabāʾ supplies an omitted promise to go and return. Al-Qushayrī stresses his care for them despite the valley's danger.
  20:10/q07/p2 The sight drew him out in an agitation he could not resist. — reasons: Al-Qushayrī gives this as another account.
20:10/q08 How is the pronoun vowel in 'to his family' read? [لِأَهْلِهِ ٱمْكُثُوٓا۟ · readings] (turns on: Pronoun dialect and phonological explanation; the sources agree that both vocalizations are transmitted.)
  20:10/q08/p1 The hāʾ is read with ḍamma. — reasons: Hamza is consistently named, also for 28:29; Ibn Mujāhid adds Ibn Saʿdān from Isḥāq al-Musayyabī, while Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī add al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa and a Nāfiʿ transmission. Al-Naḥḥās calls it original wāw retention and a dialect like marartu bihu; al-Jishumī describes transfer of the hamza vowel; al-Samīn calls it an original Hijazi dialect and reports an assimilation explanation. Qirāʾāt-Er offers dialectal leveling or syntax.
  20:10/q08/p2 The hāʾ is read with kasra. — reasons: The other readers or majority are named by Ibn Mujāhid, al-Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī and Abū Ḥayyān; al-Jishumī explains it through adjacent sukūns.
20:10/q09 What does 'ānastu' convey? [ءَانَسْتُ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the verb highlights clear reassuring sight in this scene or the broader act of finding or sensing.)
  20:10/q09/p1 I saw distinctly or perceived clearly. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba cites 4:6 for the related sense recognized; al-Ṭabarī derives it from uns and cites an Arab proverb; al-Mubarrad describes distant reassuring sight and a hunting bird noticing prey; al-ʿAjjāj and al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza furnish poetic usage. Al-Rāzī contrasts visible human beings with hidden jinn. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ counts four Moses-fire uses and a fifth at 4:6, and argues for familiarity or comfort rather than neutral sight; Iṣlāḥī says attentive observation.
  20:10/q09/p2 I found or sensed something, potentially by a sense other than sight. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Farrāʾ gloss found; al-Māwardī allows sensing something by a fire. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn say perception is broader than sight and cite a verse about faint sound; dictionaries cited by Bint al-Shāṭiʾ include hearing.
20:10/q10 Why does Moses emphasize that he has seen a fire? [إِنِّىٓ ءَانَسْتُ نَارًۭا · rhetoric]
  20:10/q10/p1 He reports certain perception to reassure his family while leaving the hoped-for benefits uncertain. — reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī contrasts certain sight with merely hoped-for fire and guidance; al-Ālūsī says inna confirms the sight even though the family expressed no doubt. Ṭabāṭabāʾ takes the singular emphatic report to imply the others did not perceive the fire.
20:10/q11 How is the first-person yāʾ of 'innī' read? [إِنِّىٓ ءَانَسْتُ · readings] (turns on: Whether the possessive yāʾ is opened in connection or kept quiescent.)
  20:10/q11/p1 It is read open, innīya. — reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī names the two Medinese, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr among five yāʾs in this passage; Qirāʾāt-Er says the change affects prosody without changing meaning. Ibn Mujāhid reports that Nāfiʿ opens the listed first-person yāʾs except in walī fīhā and akhī ushdud; Abū ʿAmr excepts walī fīhā and ḥashartanī aʿmā; Ibn Kathīr excepts walī fīhā, yassir lī amrī, lidhikrī in, ʿalā ʿaynī idh, and biraʾsī innī. Each opens the remaining listed yāʾs.
  20:10/q11/p2 It is read quiescent, innī. — reasons: Qirāʾāt-Er presents the quiescent form as the contrasting reading. Ibn

Mujāhid reports that Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim through Abū Bakr keep all the listed first-person yāʾs quiescent.
20:10/q12 Why does Moses say 'perhaps'? [لَّعَلِّىٓ · rhetoric]
  20:10/q12/p1 A firebrand or guide was hoped for, not guaranteed. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says Moses would not promise what he could not guarantee, contrasting a claim that Abraham lied for a good purpose. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī distinguish the uncertain outcome from the certain sight.
20:10/q13 How is the yāʾ of 'laʿallī' read? [لَّعَلِّىٓ ءَاتِيكُم · readings] (turns on: Opening or quiescence of the first-person yāʾ.)
  20:10/q13/p1 It is read with fatḥ, laʿalliya. — reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī names Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar across six occurrences; Qirāʾāt-Er says meaning is unchanged. Ibn Mujāhid says Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and Ibn Kathīr open the listed first-person yāʾs apart from their individually named exceptions; laʿallī is not among those exceptions.
  20:10/q13/p2 It is read quiescent, laʿallī. — reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī names the Kufans and Yaʿqūb; Qirāʾāt-Er contrasts it with open yāʾ. Ibn Mujāhid reports that Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim through Abū Bakr keep all listed first-person yāʾs quiescent.
20:10/q14 What is the 'qabas' Moses hopes to bring? [بِقَبَسٍ · meaning] (turns on: Whether qabas is specifically a flaming brand, as al-Ālūsī insists, or may also be called an ember.)
  20:10/q14/p1 A flame or burning brand taken from a larger fire, carried on a stick or wick for warmth. — reasons: Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj specify the tip of a stick or reed, and al-Zajjāj allows a wick; al-Samīn calls it a passive-sense verbal noun, a glowing end taken up. Al-Ālūsī equates it with the jadwah of 28:29 and distinguishes it from an ember. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts its guiding warmth with hostile meteors and notes iqtabasa at 57:13; a report from al-Bāqir says the family needed warmth.
  20:10/q14/p2 An ember or piece of fire to carry back. — reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow an ember, and Ibn Kathīr cites 28:29 for a glowing brand and warmth; Iṣlāḥī likewise speaks of an ember against cold.
20:10/q15 How do the related verbs for taking or giving fire and knowledge differ? [بِقَبَسٍ · meaning] (turns on: Whether usage assigns separate domains to the simple and prefixed forms or allows both in both domains.)
  20:10/q15/p1 The simple form concerns fire; the prefixed form concerns seeking or imparting knowledge. — reasons: Abū Zayd distinguishes bringing fire from seeking it; al-Mubarrad and al-Samīn distinguish giving fire from giving knowledge. These reports differ in their precise formulation.
  20:10/q15/p2 Both forms can be used for fire or knowledge. — reasons: Al-Kisāʾī allows both; al-Mubarrad says their underlying sense is one because both fire and knowledge illuminate.
20:10/q16 How is 'from it' attached grammatically? [مِّنْهَا بِقَبَسٍ · grammar] (turns on: Direct verbal attachment or an omitted circumstance describing the brand.)
  20:10/q16/p1 It attaches directly to the verb 'bring'. — reasons: Al-Samīn and Abū al-Baqāʾ, as cited by al-Ālūsī, permit this attachment.
  20:10/q16/p2 It is an omitted circumstantial qualification of the firebrand. — reasons: Al-Samīn and Abū al-Baqāʾ supply the omitted circumstance.
20:10/q17 Do the two hopes joined by 'or' exclude one another? [أَوْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the alternatives are merely listed as possibilities or explicitly compatible.)
  20:10/q17/p1 They are alternative hoped-for outcomes but need not exclude obtaining both. — reasons: Bursevī explicitly allows both; al-Ālūsī says aw prevents exclusion and presents two anticipated possibilities.
  20:10/q17/p2 They express two possible outcomes, neither yet certain. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī treats aw in the hope clause as the expression of two anticipated possibilities.
20:10/q18 What does 'upon the fire' mean? [عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ · grammar] (turns on: Whether ʿalā retains spatial elevation, stands for another local preposition, or describes an implicit guide.)
  20:10/q18/p1 On or above a nearby elevated place by the fire. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says people around a fire stand on overlooking ground; Abū Ḥayyān keeps the ordinary elevation sense, and al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow elevated ground. Al-Ālūsī says elevation becomes an idiom for a nearby place, citing Sībawayh's account of bi as contact with a nearby place.
  20:10/q18/p2 It means 'at,' 'with,' or 'by' the fire. — reasons: Ibn al-Anbārī offers these prepositional senses; al-Ālūsī says substitution is unnecessary.
  20:10/q18/p3 It is a circumstance of an implied guide located near the fire. — reasons: Some grammarians move a description before its noun and take the result to mean someone near the fire who could help the family warm itself.
20:10/q19 What guidance did Moses hope to find by the fire? [هُدًۭى · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the family's lost route and need for water call for practical directions, or the phrase suggests religious guidance; the latter is challenged using the parallel at 28:29.)
  20:10/q19/p1 A person or people to guide him along the lost road. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Suddī and others give this sense. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Wāḥidī call hudā a verbal noun in place of hādī; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī allow ellipsis 'one possessing guidance' or metonymy. Al-Suddī reasons people must tend a fire. Al-Ṭabarī permits spoken information about the route; Wahb seeks knowledge from an account. Qatāda transmits Aylah as a place attribution; al-Māwardī reports the family later stayed three days before a shepherd found them and then lived in a village forty years.
  20:10/q19/p2 A sign or source of direction revealing the route. — reasons: Al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī explicitly allow a sign, and al-Ṭabrisī says hudā names both guidance and what guides. Al-Rāzī gives a source or sign; al-Ṭabarī and Wahb allow route information.
  20:10/q19/p3 A person to lead him to water or to both water and the road. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj is cited for lost water; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report the water variant; al-Ālūsī's travel account says there was no water.
  20:10/q19/p4 Religious guidance. — reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī lists it as an alternative; Abū Ḥayyān attributes it to Mujāhid and Qatāda but calls it remote. Al-Ālūsī says their minds remained on religion, but rejects the fit with the family's needs and 28:29. Asad sees a possible symbol of Moses' dawning spiritual need.
20:10/q20 How is 'hudā' read at a pause? [هُدًۭى · readings] (turns on: Whether the final alif is merely a pause substitute for tanwīn or can be treated as a lexical ending permitting imāla.)
  20:10/q20/p1 Pause without imāla, preserving the alif replacing tanwīn. — reasons: Al-Samīn calls this better; Abū al-Baqāʾ prefers alif without inclination.
  20:10/q20/p2 Pause with imāla. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports explanations that tanwīn resembles a lexical ending, that the ending remains without tanwīn, or that a pausal form is used in all cases.
20:10/q21 What grammatical role can the clause of hope play? [لَّعَلِّىٓ ءَاتِيكُم أَوْ أَجِدُ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the hope clause explains the command, describes Moses, or modifies the fire; al-Ālūsī rejects the last.)
  20:10/q21/p1 It gives the reason for telling the family to stay. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī lists this as one analysis.
  20:10/q21/p2 It describes Moses' state as he went toward the fire. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī lists a circumstantial analysis.
  20:10/q21/p3 It is an adjective describing the fire. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports a defense from a poetic comparison, but calls the analysis flawed.
20:10/q22 Why repeat 'the fire' instead of using a pronoun? [عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ · rhetoric]
  20:10/q22/p1 Naming the fire explains why someone offering guidance might be found there. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī says people commonly gather around a fire; al-Suddī makes the same practical inference.
20:10/q23 How does this telling relate to other tellings of Moses' fire? [* · links]
  20:10/q23/p1 Parallel passages vary their wording while recounting the same episode. — reasons: Al-Bāqillānī cites Ṭā Hā, al-Naml and al-Qaṣaṣ as varied expression that broadens the challenge to produce comparable discourse, citing 27:8, 28:29 and 52:34; he says paraphrase reveals the loss of Qurʾānic wording. Al-Burhān notes Ṭā Hā's atāhā against al-Naml's jāʾahā. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes Moses' shihāb qabs in 27:7 and 28:29 from hostile meteors in 15:18, 37:10 and 72:9; she records al-Rāghib's bright-flame sense and Arabic applications to stars, snow mountains and white streaks.
  20:10/q23/p2 The parallel passages clarify that Moses sought warmth and a glowing brand. — reasons: Al-Yaḥyā cites 27:7; Ibn Kathīr and others cite 28:29 for darkness, cold and the brand.
20:10/q24 How does the episode serve the surrounding sūra? [* · links] (turns on: The sources emphasize consolation, literary and narrative sequence, or the beginning of the prophetic call.)
  20:10/q24/p1 It consoles Muhammad through Moses' trials and God's support. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says the episode amid Quraysh's persecution promises Muhammad's eventual ascendancy and weakening of unbelievers' schemes, urging endurance in worship and effort. Al-Biqāʿī prefers a coherence reading in which all creation belongs to God and divine aid overcomes difficulty; Moses' rescue, Pharaoh's ruin and Israel's emergence exemplify it.
  20:10/q24/p2 Moses follows mention of Muhammad because God used the apparent fire to draw him from his family. — reasons: Al-Qushayrī says the fire was a means rather than the ultimate aim; al-Bāqillānī praises the exact ordering and smooth transitions between stories.
  20:10/q24/p3 The episode begins Moses' call to prophethood in the sacred valley. — reasons: Iṣlāḥī places the return from Midian at Ṭuwā, where Moses receives prophethood; Kuranyolu calls the light an entry into divine presence.
20:10/q25 What

 inward meaning is given to the fire and Moses' hopes? [* · inward] (turns on: Different inward readings identify the fire with the Holy Spirit, divine manifestation, or spiritual awakening.)
  20:10/q25/p1 The fire is the Holy Spirit illuminating souls, and the family are Moses' faculties. — reasons: Al-Qāshānī says the faculties remain still as sensory activity quiets; the firebrand is a luminous benefit to them, while finding a guide is gaining knowledge and gnosis leading to truth.
  20:10/q25/p2 God appeared in the desired form of fire to draw Moses toward Him. — reasons: Bursevī transmits some Sufis' explanation that another form might have made Moses turn away; his poem says Moses did not yet recognize the divine manifestation in light and speech.
  20:10/q25/p3 The fire symbolizes rising spiritual certainty. — reasons: The Study Quran adds the mountain of God, Horeb, from Exodus; Asad treats the lost road as a possible symbol of spiritual need and the fire as a burning-bush allegory.
20:10/q26 How did Moses recognize the divine call at the fire? [* · theology] (turns on: Inference from the character of the speech versus direct divinely given recognition.)
  20:10/q26/p1 He inferred it from the speech's ordered structure and composition. — reasons: Al-Qushayrī says this recognition came when he tried to take a flame.
  20:10/q26/p2 God made His speech known through special inspiration without inference. — reasons: Al-Qushayrī reports this alternative.
20:10/q27 Why did Moses remove his sandals, according to related reports? [* · reports] (turns on: The reports appeal to the sandals' material, the valley's blessing, or symbolic humility.)
  20:10/q27/p1 They were made from donkey hide. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī transmits Ibn Masʿūd's report from the Prophet specifying a dead donkey and a variant specifying untanned hide; al-Ḥasan contrasts this with Muhammad's prayer in sandals.
  20:10/q27/p2 His bare feet could touch and receive the blessed ground. — reasons: ʿIkrima and Mujāhid call it twice sanctified; another explanation singles out his heels.
  20:10/q27/p3 Barefootedness expresses humility or detachment from family. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī reports these explanations, adding that shoes in dreams signify a wife.
  20:10/q27/p4 Removing sandals was associated with the sacred valley. — reasons: Abū al-Aḥwaṣ reports Ibn Masʿūd joking to Abū Mūsā, who had removed sandals before prayer, 'Are you in the sacred valley?'
20:10/q28 How are other nearby words and the preceding question explained? [* · meaning] (turns on: These are separate contextual observations included in the collected notes.)
  20:10/q28/p1 The preceding hal keeps its ordinary confirmatory interrogative sense. — reasons: Al-Samīn also reports proposed readings as qad or as negation.
  20:10/q28/p2 Akhfaytu can mean concealed or revealed, while khafaytu means revealed only. — reasons: Al-Ṭabrisī records the distinction and also glosses radā and taraddā as destruction.
  20:10/q28/p3 Saʿy means swift movement or action, and radā and ardā concern perishing and destroying. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān cites Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma's poetry for ardā.
  20:10/q28/p4 The king's dream in Joseph was true inspiration, not the confused dreams claimed by his court. — reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 12:43–44 in her wider discussion of distinctive Qurʾānic diction.
20:10/q29 What view of divine istiwāʾ does the source favor in the preceding context? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether istiwāʾ is explained as power or as a distinct act or attribute.)
  20:10/q29/p1 It means divine power. — reasons: Al-Jishumī prefers Abū ʿAlī's explanation and calls the Kullābī account of a separate act or attribute named istiwāʾ unintelligible.
  20:10/q29/p2 It is an act or attribute called istiwāʾ. — reasons: Al-Jishumī reports the Kullābī account solely to dispute its intelligibility.

[DURR-FULL:v5p553/r5] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · قتادة | reports | Qatada explains ‘I perceive a fire’ as ‘I sense a fire,’ and seeking guidance there as asking who will guide him.
